src: Peer-reviewed papers cited on each card (Nature, Science, PNAS and others)
dt: Dwarf dinosaurs live on Hațeg Island in the European sea
On an island of roughly 80,000 sq km, the sauropod Magyarosaurus grew only about 6 m long as an adult and the duckbill Telmatosaurus about 5 m: island dwarfing, as Franz Nopcsa first proposed.
Benton et al. 2010, Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology
Balaur, a raptor with two killer claws on each foot, hunts on Hațeg
Balaur bondoc from Romania's Sebeș Formation was about 1.8 to 2.5 m long and about 15 kg. Unlike other raptors it had big sickle claws on both its first and second toes.
A duck-like bird honks in a warm Antarctica
Vegavis from Cape Lamb on Vega Island (69.2 to 68.4 million years old) preserves the oldest known bird voice box. Its shape suggests goose-like honks rather than song.
Giant Mosasaurus hunts the chalk seas near Maastricht
Mosasaurus hoffmannii, a sea lizard up to about 12 m long, is named from a skull found near Maastricht in 1778. Cuvier later used it to argue that whole species can go extinct.
The oldest known modern bird lives on a Belgian coast
Asteriornis maastrichtensis, the Wonderchicken from Eben-Emael, is 66.8 to 66.7 million years old. It weighed about 394 g, had long legs and is related to both chickens and ducks.
Titanosaurs lay eggs in big nesting colonies in central India
92 nests holding 256 eggs were found in the Lameta Formation of Dhar District. The nests sit close together, so these giants nested in colonies.
Dinosaur dung shows that grasses already grow in India
Titanosaur dung from Pisdura holds tiny silica grains from at least five kinds of grass, so grasses had already spread across the southern continents before the dinosaurs died out.
One of the first hoofed placental mammals appears in Montana
Protungulatum coombsi from the Hell Creek Formation lived at least 300,000 years before the asteroid. It is one of the oldest possible placental mammals, perhaps an early relative of hoofed animals.
Archibald et al. 2011, Journal of Mammalian Evolution
Deccan volcanoes warm the oceans just before the dinosaurs end
The Late Maastrichtian warming began about 66.34 million years ago, some 300,000 years before the impact. Deep water in the South Atlantic warmed by about 4 °C.
Hull et al. 2020, Science; ODP Site 1262
Antarctic sea life suffers a first extinction pulse as seas warm
Shells from Seymour Island record warming of about 7.8 °C while 10 species vanished, most of them seafloor dwellers. A second pulse at the impact wiped out the last ammonites there.
Ferns briefly take over burned forests after the asteroid
In New Mexico's Raton Basin, fern spores suddenly replace flowering-plant pollen right above the boundary clay: a fern spike. Ferns were the first plants back after the disaster.
A second asteroid digs the Nadir crater off West Africa
The Nadir crater lies under the seafloor about 400 km off Guinea-Bissau. It is about 9 km wide, was probably made by an asteroid about 400 m across, and is close in age to Chicxulub.
Mammal variety doubles in the forests of Colorado
At Corral Bluffs the number of mammal species roughly doubled within about 100,000 years of the impact. The largest mammals were still under about 9 kg.
One of the earliest primates scurries through Montana
Teeth of Purgatorius mckeeveri from the Hell Creek area date to about 105,000 to 139,000 years after the asteroid. It was rat-sized, about 37 g, and lived in trees.
Wilson Mantilla et al. 2021, Royal Society Open Science
The Dan-C2 event briefly warms the recovering world
Twin carbon-isotope spikes about 65.8 and 65.7 million years ago mark a short, mild warming called Dan-C2, found in ocean rocks and in lake and river beds of China's Nanxiong Basin.
Mammals grow three times bigger in Colorado's forests
About 300,000 years after the impact, the largest mammals at Corral Bluffs were three times heavier than before, as the forests grew richer again.
An asteroid blasts the 24 km Boltysh crater in Ukraine
Argon dating puts the Boltysh impact about 65.39 million years ago, a few hundred thousand years after Chicxulub. It left a crater about 24 km wide in central Ukraine.
Mammals reach wolf size as the first beans appear
About 700,000 years after the impact, mammals at Corral Bluffs such as Taeniolabis reached about 45 kg, at the same time as the oldest known fossils of legumes, the bean family.
A flash flood buries a family of tiny opossum relatives in Bolivia
At Tiupampa, 35 Pucadelphys skeletons were found together: males, females and young. They are the oldest evidence of mammals living in groups.
The Latest Danian Event warms Earth's oceans
The first heat spike of the age of mammals lasted about 200,000 years. Two carbon pulses warmed surface and deep seas by about 2 to 3 °C and made seawater more acidic.
Kupoupou, a penguin with modern legs, swims off the Chatham Islands
Kupoupou stilwelli from the Takatika Grit (62.5 to 60 million years old) is the earliest penguin known with legs and feet shaped like those of living penguins.
Waimanu, one of the first penguins, dives off New Zealand
Waimanu manneringi from the Waipara Greensand was already flightless and dived using its wings. It stood roughly 1 m tall, but its wings were less flipper-like than today's penguins'.
Slack et al. 2006, Molecular Biology and Evolution
The oldest known elephant relative lives in Morocco
Eritherium azzouzorum from the Ouled Abdoun phosphate basin weighed only about 5 kg, between a rabbit and a fox. It is the oldest and most primitive known member of the elephant order.
A French crater lake preserves insects, leaves and furry primates
The Menat maar lake preserves leaves, insects, turtles, birds and Plesiadapis with outlines of fur. Many leaves are chewed by insects, so Europe's forests had recovered.
Titanoboa, the biggest snake ever, swims in Colombian swamps
Titanoboa cerrejonensis from the Cerrejón coal mine was about 12.8 m long and weighed about 1,135 kg. A snake that big needs a hot climate, around 30 to 34 °C.
The first true rainforest of the Americas grows in Colombia
More than 2,000 fossil leaves from Cerrejón show palms, legumes, laurels and other families growing together, the oldest known Neotropical rainforest.
Kumimanu, the heaviest penguin ever, swims off New Zealand
Kumimanu fordycei from North Otago (59.5 to 55.5 million years old) weighed an estimated 150 kg or so, more than three times an emperor penguin.
Ksepka et al. 2023, Journal of Paleontology
Early horses shrink as the planet heats up in Wyoming
The early horse Sifrhippus shrank by about 30%, from about 5.4 to 3.9 kg, in the first 130,000 years of the heat spike, then grew to about 7 kg as the world cooled again.
Tiny primates spread from Asia to Europe and America in a heatwave
Teilhardina, one of the oldest true primates, appears in Asia, then Belgium, then Wyoming within about 25,000 years during the heat spike that opened the Eocene.
A mouse-sized primate leaps through trees in China
Archicebus achilles, from an ancient lake bed in Hubei, weighed under 30 g. It is the oldest well-preserved primate skeleton, close to the split between tarsiers and monkeys and apes.
A second heat spike hits the oceans
Eocene Thermal Maximum 2 (the Elmo event) warmed Arctic surface seas by 3 to 5 °C and lasted under 200,000 years. Its timing follows a cycle in Earth's orbit.
Earth enters its hottest stretch since the dinosaurs died
In the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, about 53 to 49 million years ago, Earth's average surface temperature was about 27 °C, roughly double today's.
Inglis et al. 2020, Climate of the Past
Alligators and giant tortoises live near the North Pole
Early Eocene rocks on Ellesmere Island hold alligators, giant tortoises and hippo-like Coryphodon. Their teeth and shells show summers of 19 to 20 °C and winters of only 0 to 3.5 °C.
Eberle et al. 2010, Earth and Planetary Science Letters
Early bats flutter over a lake in Wyoming
Onychonycteris finneyi from the Green River Formation had claws on all five fingers and short wings, but lacked the ear of echolocating bats: bats may have flown before they could echolocate.
Millions of fish are buried in Wyoming's Fossil Lake
Fossil Lake, now Fossil Butte National Monument, preserves fish, bats and stingrays. Its herring-like Knightia is one of the most common vertebrate fossils in the world.
Floating ferns carpet the Arctic Ocean
Layers of the water fern Azolla in cores from the Lomonosov Ridge show huge blooms on a freshened Arctic Ocean for about 800,000 years, which may have helped draw carbon dioxide from the air.
A wolf-like animal starts the long journey to become a whale
Pakicetus, from the Kuldana Formation of northern Pakistan, was a four-legged mammal 1 to 2 m long. Its ear bones show it was an early relative of whales.
A volcanic crater lake forms in Germany and becomes a fossil trap
The Messel maar erupted about 48 million years ago. Its lake mud, laid down over about 640,000 years, holds more than 1,400 kinds of fossils, some with stomach contents or original colours.
Lenz et al. 2015, International Journal of Earth Sciences; UNESCO 1995
Ida, a lemur-like primate, sinks into the Messel lake
Darwinius masillae, nicknamed Ida, is a 95% complete primate skeleton about 58 cm long including the tail. She died young, at roughly nine months old.
Thumb-sized early monkey relatives live in China
Cave fillings near Shanghuang, Jiangsu, hold Eosimias, an early anthropoid, and primates from 10 to 1,000 grams. Some were half the size of a mouse.
Beard et al. 1994, Nature; Gebo et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution
Nuts and fruits fall in a steamy Oregon jungle
The Clarno Nut Beds hold more than 175 species of fossil fruits and nuts from a rainforest that got about 3 m of rain a year, home to early horses and land crocodiles.
John Day Fossil Beds National Monument
A four-legged whale swims all the way to Peru
Peregocetus pacificus, 3.4 to 4 m long, could walk on land and swam like an otter. Found at Playa Media Luna, it is the oldest whale fossil in the Americas.
African rodents raft across the ocean to South America
Teeth from Contamana, Peru, at least 41 million years old, are South America's oldest rodents. They are closest to African rodents, so the animals crossed the Atlantic.
Antoine et al. 2012, Proceedings of the Royal Society B
The first members of the dog family appear in North America
Hesperocyon is the oldest known canid. Its earliest teeth come from Lac Pelletier, Saskatchewan, and it later became common across the White River badlands.
Bryant 1992, Journal of Paleontology; Wang 1994, Bulletin AMNH
A burst of carbon dioxide warms the middle Eocene
In the Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum, seas off Tasmania warmed by 3 to 6 °C for about 400,000 years while carbon dioxide rose two to three times.
Legged whales swim in a warm sea that is now Egypt's desert
Wadi Al-Hitan holds hundreds of fossils of early whales like Basilosaurus and Dorudon, some with small hind legs. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
Giant penguins taller than people swim off Antarctica
Palaeeudyptes klekowskii from Seymour Island's La Meseta Formation stood about 2 m tall and weighed roughly 115 kg.
Huge rhino-like brontotheres roam the South Dakota floodplains
The Chadron Formation of Badlands National Park, about 37 to 34 million years old, holds giant brontotheres and alligators from a hot, wet floodplain; later layers record a cooler savanna.
The first baleen whale still has teeth
Mystacodon selenensis from Peru's Pisco Basin is the oldest known baleen-whale relative. It was about 3.75 to 4 m long and probably sucked prey up from the seafloor.
Asian mammals sweep into Europe as old species vanish
In the Grande Coupure, sudden cooling at the start of the Oligocene came with the loss of European mammals like Palaeotherium and Anoplotherium, replaced by newcomers from Asia.
Hooker et al. 2004, Journal of the Geological Society
Eurotrochilus inexpectatus from a clay pit at Frauenweiler is the oldest modern-type hummingbird. Its skeletons are only about 4 cm long.
A current begins to circle Antarctica
The Tasmanian Gateway had opened deep by about 33.5 million years ago; around 30 million years ago it moved into the westerly winds and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current began.
Monkey and ape ancestors climb trees in Egypt
Aegyptopithecus, about 6.7 kg, lived in Egypt's Fayum forests 30.2 to 29.5 million years ago, before apes and Old World monkeys split.
Simons et al. 2007, PNAS; Seiffert 2006, PNAS
Monkeys reach South America after crossing from Africa
Teeth of Perupithecus from Santa Rosa, Peru, resemble African primates. Zircon dating puts the site at no older than 29.6 million years.
Bond et al. 2015, Nature; Campbell et al. 2021, PNAS
Giant hornless rhinos taller than giraffes roam China
Paraceratherium linxiaense from the Linxia Basin in Gansu had a skull over a metre long. Giant rhinos of its kind stood about 5 m at the shoulder.
The oldest known ape lives in Tanzania
Rukwapithecus fleaglei, the oldest ape, and Nsungwepithecus, the oldest Old World monkey, both come from 25.2-million-year-old rocks in the Rukwa Rift.
Australia's Riversleigh rainforest fills with odd marsupials
Riversleigh's fossils run from about 25 million years ago to the present; more than 250 fossil assemblages record rainforest marsupials. It became a UNESCO site in 1994.
UNESCO World Heritage List; IUCN World Heritage Outlook
The first true cat prowls the forests of France
Proailurus, from Saint-Gérand-le-Puy and Quercy, is widely thought to be the first true cat. It weighed about 9 kg, a little more than a house cat.
Antarctic ice surges briefly as Earth's orbit lines up
At the Oligocene–Miocene boundary a nearly circular orbit and a steady axis tilt coincided, causing a short glaciation, Mi-1, when Antarctica's ice sheet grew.
Africa and Arabia meet Eurasia, making a land bridge for animals
When Afro-Arabia hit Eurasia about 19 to 15 million years ago, gomphotheres and other elephant relatives walked out of Africa, and cats and other carnivores walked in.
Harzhauser et al. 2007; Cantalapiedra et al. 2021, Nature Ecology and Evolution
Proconsul, an early tailless ape, lives on Rusinga Island in Kenya
Rusinga Island's fossil beds in Lake Victoria are about 18 million years old. In 1948 Mary Leakey found the first complete skull of the early ape Proconsul there.
Earth heats up in the Miocene Climatic Optimum
From about 17 to 14.7 million years ago Earth was roughly 3 to 4 °C warmer than today, the warmest stretch of the last 20 million years.
Steinthorsdottir et al. 2021, Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology
A toothed platypus swims in Riversleigh's rainforest streams
Riversleigh in Queensland gave a skull of Obdurodon dicksoni, a platypus relative that still had teeth as an adult, about 15 million years old.
Archer et al. 1992; UNESCO World Heritage List
Sivapithecus, a cousin of orangutans, lives in Pakistan's forests
Sivapithecus fossils from the Siwalik rocks go back about 12.2 million years. A partial face from the Potwar Plateau looks strikingly like an orangutan's.
Volcanic ash smothers rhinos and horses at a Nebraska waterhole
Ash from a supervolcano in the Bruneau-Jarbidge area of Idaho, about 1,400 km away, buried a waterhole. More than 100 skeletons of the rhino Teleoceras have been dug up there.
Danuvius, an ape that may have walked on two legs, lives in Germany
Fossils from the Hammerschmiede clay pit in Bavaria are 11.62 million years old. Danuvius weighed about 23 kg; its finders argue it walked upright along branches, which others dispute.
Livyatan, a giant sperm whale with huge teeth, hunts off Peru
The skull from Cerro Colorado in Peru's Pisco Formation is about 3 m long with teeth up to 36 cm. The whale may have been 13.5 to 17.5 m long.
Heat-loving tropical grasses spread across Asia and Africa
Carbon in ancient soils and in horse and elephant teeth shows C4 grasses spreading in Pakistan from about 7.8 million years ago, part of a worldwide shift between 8 and 6 million years ago.
Toumaï, one of the oldest known members of the human family, lives in Chad
The Sahelanthropus tchadensis skull from Toros-Menalla in Chad's Djurab Desert is dated to 7.04 ± 0.18 million years from beryllium isotopes in the sediments around it.
Dozens of whales strand again and again on a beach in Chile
Cerro Ballena near Caldera holds more than 40 baleen whales and other sea animals in four layers 6 to 9 million years old. Toxic algae blooms probably caused the repeated strandings.
Pyenson et al. 2014, Proceedings of the Royal Society B
Orrorin, an early human relative built for walking, lives in Kenya
Orrorin tugenensis fossils from the Tugen Hills are about 6.2 to 6.0 million years old. Its thigh bones suggest it walked upright but still climbed trees.
Senut et al. 2001; Smithsonian Human Origins Program
Ardipithecus kadabba, an early hominin, walks in Ethiopia
Ardipithecus kadabba lived about 5.8 to 5.2 million years ago in the Middle Awash. It is known from 11 specimens of at least five individuals; a toe bone suggests upright walking.
A red panda and an early wolverine live by a forest pond in Tennessee
The Gray Fossil Site, found by road builders in 2000, is a 4.9 to 4.5 million year old sinkhole pond with the red panda Pristinailurus, the oldest known wolverine, tapirs, rhinos and alligators.
Ardi, who climbed trees and walked upright, lives in Ethiopia
Ardi is a partial skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus from Aramis in the Middle Awash, about 4.4 million years old. She stood about 1.2 m tall and was described in 11 papers in 2009.
Australopithecus anamensis walks upright beside a Kenyan lake
Australopithecus anamensis lived about 4.2 to 3.8 million years ago at Kanapoi and Allia Bay near Lake Turkana. Its shin and ankle show it regularly walked on two legs.
A nearly complete skull shows the face of Lucy's ancestor
The MRD skull of Australopithecus anamensis from Woranso-Mille, Ethiopia, is about 3.8 million years old. It shows anamensis and Lucy's species overlapped for at least 100,000 years.
Little Foot, an early human relative, ends up in a South African cave
Little Foot (StW 573) is an unusually complete Australopithecus skeleton from the Sterkfontein Caves. Burial dating gives an age of 3.67 ± 0.16 million years.
Early humans leave footprints in volcanic ash at Laetoli
Found in 1978, this trail is almost 27 m long with about 70 footprints of upright walkers, probably Australopithecus afarensis, in ash about 3.6 million years old.
Abel shows early humans lived far west of the Rift Valley in Chad
The jaw known as Abel (Australopithecus bahrelghazali), found at Koro Toro in 1995, is dated to 3.58 ± 0.27 million years, about 2,500 km west of the Rift Valley.
Brunet et al. 1995, Nature; Lebatard et al. 2008, PNAS
Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced human relative, lives by Lake Turkana
The KNM-WT 40000 skull found at Lomekwi in 1999 is about 3.5 million years old. Its flat face suggested a second hominin lineage living alongside Lucy's species.
Zebra-like Hagerman horses, early members of the modern horse genus, roam Idaho
Hagerman's 4 to 3 million year old beds hold the world's largest collection of Equus simplicidens, one of the oldest species of Equus, including more than 100 skulls.
A hominin with a grasping big toe climbs trees in Ethiopia
A partial foot from Burtele at Woranso-Mille, about 3.4 million years old, has an opposable big toe for climbing: a second kind of hominin lived beside Lucy's species.
Someone makes the oldest known stone tools at Lomekwi, Kenya
Found in 2011 near Lake Turkana, the Lomekwi 3 cores, flakes and anvils are 3.3 million years old, about 700,000 years older than the earliest Oldowan tools.
The mid-Pliocene warm period makes Earth about 2 °C warmer than today
From about 3.264 to 3.025 million years ago Earth was roughly 2 °C warmer than today, with carbon dioxide close to today's level. Scientists use it to test climate models.
USGS PRISM project; Dowsett et al. 2016, Climate of the Past
The oldest known member of our genus Homo leaves a jaw in Ethiopia
The LD 350-1 jawbone, found at Ledi-Geraru in 2013, is about 2.8 to 2.75 million years old, the earliest known fossil of the genus Homo.
The Black Skull shows a big-jawed human relative in Kenya
Found in West Turkana in 1985, the Black Skull (KNM-WT 17000) of Paranthropus aethiopicus is about 2.5 million years old, with a huge crest for chewing muscles; manganese stained it black.
